CELL BIOLOGY · MILESTONE 5 OF 12

Required Practical 1: Microscopy
Why am I learning this?

Careful focusing, drawing and labelling produce useful evidence about cells. These skills prepare you to observe real tissue with your teacher.

What should I already understand?

Microscope theory, cell structures, magnification and scale.

Previous: Microscopy
Next recommended: Chromosomes, cell division and stem cells

Method, observations and scale

Prepare a thin specimen on a slide, add a suitable stain and lower a coverslip carefully. Start with a low-power objective, focus, then increase magnification. Draw clear outlines and label visible structures. Magnification = image size ÷ real size; use the same units.

RP01 requires observing, drawing and labelling a selection of plant and animal cells with a magnification scale. Use a teacher-approved thin onion epidermis sample and a prepared animal-cell slide, such as a stained cheek epithelial slide; a fresh cheek sample is not required. Prepared slides provide animal evidence without assuming permission or procedures for collecting human samples. Under teacher instructions, spread a thin onion peel flat in a drop of water, use dilute iodine if specified to improve contrast, and lower a coverslip at an angle to reduce trapped air. A prepared animal slide may already be stained with methylene blue; do not add stain or a coverslip to a sealed prepared slide. These are suitable examples, not a requirement to use one named specimen or stain. Wear eye protection when handling stains, avoid skin/eye contact, wash hands, handle slide edges carefully and follow school spill and broken-glass procedures; do not handle broken glass. Start with the lowest objective. Adjust illumination, locate and centre cells, use coarse then fine focus at low power, and use fine focus when moving to higher power. Watch clearance when positioning the lens; never drive it into the slide. Observe several cells from each specimen and record specimen, objective/eyepiece magnification, visible structures and any variation. Draw large, clear, single outlines with appropriate proportions, a title and straight non-crossing label lines; no invented features or artistic shading. Include total magnification (eyepiece × objective) or a calibrated magnification scale/scale bar; explain which value describes the microscope and which describes a resized drawing. Use provided/calibrated size information rather than guessing actual cell size. Plant onion cells show a wall and large vacuole; a stained nucleus may be seen. Animal cells lack cell walls and chloroplasts. Onion bulb epidermis normally has no chloroplasts, unlike photosynthetic leaf cells. Do not claim ribosomes are visible with this light microscope or mistake air bubbles for nuclei. If a boundary is unclear, record that limitation rather than inventing it. Compare plant and animal observations, noting shared and different structures. Review the model drawing and scale task in practice. This online support prepares you for the practical; actual observations require laboratory work.

Preparing for the physical required practical

Use a light microscope to observe, draw and label plant and animal cells, including a magnification scale.

Review the theory in the previous milestone. Follow your teacher’s safety instructions in the laboratory. Reading this guidance or using the Osmosis Lab does not complete the physical required practical.

Controls and fair comparisons

Use consistent illumination/preparation when comparing specimens. Record eyepiece and objective magnification; measure with a calibrated scale or supplied reference. Repeat observations across several cells, distinguishing biological variation from preparation artefacts.

Analysing results and evaluating errors

Model observation record: onion epidermis — box-like adjoining cells and walls, large clear vacuolar region, stained nucleus if visible, no chloroplasts expected. Prepared animal epithelium — irregular outlines, cytoplasm and stained nucleus, no wall. Draw what the slide actually shows. A 10 mm drawing of a measured 20 µm cell is ×500: 10/0.020 = 500. Label the drawing and include a 20 µm scale bar spanning that cell; resizing changes the drawing magnification.

Start low and centre before increasing power; fine focus protects the lens/slide at high power. A magnification value is not a length; a scale bar needs a real-length label. Stains improve contrast, not resolving power. Never add ribosomes or chloroplasts just because a textbook schematic shows them.

What should I demonstrate?

Describe a safe method, draw and label observations, calculate magnification and evaluate observation errors.

Demonstrate understanding through existing practice and assessment. The existing scoring and independent Osmosis Lab checks are unchanged; visiting a milestone is not evidence of mastery.

CELL BIOLOGY · MILESTONE 6 OF 12

Chromosomes, cell division and stem cells
Why am I learning this?

New cells let you grow and repair damaged tissue. Chromosomes explain how genetic information is copied, while stem cells explain possible treatments and their risks.

What should I already understand?

Nucleus and DNA as genetic material; structures and specialised cell functions.

Previous: Required Practical 1: Microscopy
Next recommended: Diffusion

Chromosomes and DNA

For the existing DNA explanation and paired chromosomes, open Inheritance → DNA, genes and chromosomes, then Sex chromosomes and inheritance. Chromosomes in the nucleus are made of DNA; each carries many genes. Body-cell chromosomes are normally in pairs.

The cell cycle and mitosis

The three overall cell-cycle stages are: (1) the cell grows, increases sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria, and copies DNA so there are two copies of each chromosome; (2) mitosis separates one set of chromosomes to each end and the nucleus divides; (3) the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide, forming two genetically identical daughter cells with the original chromosome number. Growth of an embryo or root and replacement of damaged skin involve mitosis. You do not need the named phases of mitosis.

Differentiation

Division increases cell number; differentiation produces specialised cells with different sub-cellular structures and functions. Most animal cells differentiate early in development; many plant cells retain differentiation potential throughout life. In mature animals division is mainly for repair and replacement. This is why a specialised nerve cell and muscle cell differ even though they normally share genetic information. Growth can involve division, enlargement and differentiation; these are different processes.

Stem cells and their uses

A stem cell is undifferentiated: it can divide to make more stem cells and can give rise to differentiated cells. Embryonic stem cells can produce most human cell types. Adult bone-marrow stem cells produce several types of blood cell; their range is more limited. Plant meristems contain cells that can divide and differentiate into any plant cell type throughout life. Potential treatments include replacing insulin-producing cells in diabetes or damaged nerve cells in paralysis; potential is not a guaranteed cure. In therapeutic cloning an embryo with the patient's genes supplies stem cells, so cells derived from it are not rejected as genetically foreign. Stem-cell use can transfer viral infection, and uncontrolled cell division may form tumours. Embryo use also raises ethical or religious objections. Evaluate evidence of likely benefit, risk and alternatives; explain reasons rather than treating one ethical opinion as the correct answer. Meristem cloning can produce many identical plants quickly and economically: it can preserve a rare species or multiply a crop with a useful inherited feature such as disease resistance. Stem-cell laboratory techniques are not required here.

Summary: growth and repair

Before mitosis, DNA is copied. Chromosomes are separated and the cell divides, producing two genetically identical daughter cells for growth, repair or asexual reproduction. Stem cells can divide and differentiate. Embryonic stem cells can form many cell types; adult stem cells have a more limited range. Consider benefits, rejection or tumour risks, and ethical arguments when evaluating treatment.



What should I demonstrate?

Explain chromosomes, the cell cycle and mitosis; distinguish division from differentiation and evaluate stem-cell uses.

Demonstrate understanding through existing practice and assessment. The existing scoring and independent Osmosis Lab checks are unchanged; visiting a milestone is not evidence of mastery.

CELL BIOLOGY · MILESTONE 7 OF 12

Diffusion
Why am I learning this?

Oxygen reaches cells and wastes leave by diffusion. Understanding random particle movement explains why substances spread without a pump.

What should I already understand?

Cell membranes; the particle and concentration introduction below.

Previous: Chromosomes, cell division and stem cells
Next recommended: Surface area and exchange

Before diffusion: particles and concentration

Substances are made of particles. Particles in gases and solutions move randomly in all directions. Concentration means the amount of a substance in a given volume. A concentration gradient is a difference in concentration between two places. Random movement can produce more particles moving from the higher-concentration side to the lower-concentration side overall: this is net movement.

Diffusion overview

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a higher concentration to a lower concentration. It is faster with a steeper concentration gradient, a higher temperature or a larger surface area.

Particle movement and diffusion

Diffusion is the spreading of gas particles or dissolved particles by random movement, producing net movement down a concentration gradient. Particles still move in both directions; at equal concentrations there is no net movement. Oxygen diffuses into respiring cells from a higher concentration outside; carbon dioxide can diffuse out where it is produced. Urea, a waste substance, diffuses from cells into blood plasma and is carried to the kidneys for excretion. A steeper concentration difference increases net movement; higher temperature increases particle motion; a larger membrane area permits more particles to cross at once. Diffusion does not require energy from respiration.

What should I demonstrate?

Describe net movement down a concentration gradient and explain factors affecting diffusion.

CELL BIOLOGY · MILESTONE 8 OF 12

Surface area and exchange
Why am I learning this?

A large animal needs specialised exchange surfaces to supply all its cells. Surface-area-to-volume reasoning explains why lungs and gills have large, thin surfaces.

What should I already understand?

Diffusion, concentration gradients and cell size.

Previous: Diffusion
Next recommended: Osmosis

Why exchange surfaces are needed

Thin exchange surfaces shorten the diffusion distance. Larger organisms have a smaller surface-area-to-volume ratio and need specialised exchange and transport systems.



Exchange adaptations

Exchange surfaces must meet demand. Alveoli in lungs have a large total area, thin walls, a good blood supply and ventilation; ventilation and blood flow maintain oxygen/carbon-dioxide gradients. Fish gill filaments and lamellae provide a large area and short diffusion path; blood flow and water moving over the gills maintain gas gradients. No detailed counter-current mechanism is needed here. Villi and microvilli increase small-intestine absorption area; a thin surface shortens the path and blood flow carries absorbed substances away. Root hairs increase contact area with soil for water and ion uptake. Thin leaves give a short gas pathway; stomata permit gas movement and air spaces expose a large area of mesophyll to gases. Photosynthesis can maintain inward carbon-dioxide and outward oxygen gradients; cells also respire, so direction depends on conditions. Plants do not have blood: do not transfer animal ventilation/blood-supply explanations uncritically to leaves and roots. In an unfamiliar organism, justify each adaptation using area, path length or maintenance of gradients rather than simply naming the organ. Use the existing Organisation lessons for alveoli, villi, leaf tissues and plant transport context.

Surface-area-to-volume reasoning

A cube with side 1 has surface area 6 and volume 1: its ratio is 6:1. Doubling the side gives area 24 and volume 8, a ratio of 3:1. The decreasing ratio helps explain why diffusion alone becomes insufficient as organisms get larger.

A single-celled organism often has a relatively large surface-area-to-volume ratio and a short distance from its surroundings to its interior, allowing diffusion to meet demand. As an organism grows, volume (and demand) increases faster than surface area, so specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems become necessary. Compare equal-volume shapes as well as different sizes. For a rectangular model, surface area = 2(length × width + length × height + width × height); volume = length × width × height. A cube with side 2 has area 24 and volume 8, so SA:V is 3:1. A flat 1 × 2 × 4 model also has volume 8 but area 2(2+4+8)=28, giving 3.5:1; it has more exchange area for the same volume and a shorter path across its thin dimension. Area uses squared units and volume cubed units; the ratio is conventionally reported as SA:V. Shape models simplify real organisms, whose surfaces may fold and whose cells differ in activity.

What should I demonstrate?

Calculate and compare surface-area-to-volume ratios; explain how exchange adaptations support diffusion.

CELL BIOLOGY · MILESTONE 9 OF 12

Osmosis
Why am I learning this?

Water movement can make plant cells firm or cause them to lose water. Osmosis explains wilting plants and why potato tissue changes mass in different solutions.

What should I already understand?

Diffusion, concentration gradients, cell membranes and exchange.

Previous: Surface area and exchange
Next recommended: Required Practical 2: Osmosis

Water movement overview

Osmosis is the net movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. Water entering a plant cell helps make it turgid.



Osmosis and cells

Osmosis is specifically the net diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. The membrane permits water through but restricts some dissolved substances. In dilute surroundings, water can enter cells. A plant cell becomes turgid as its contents push against its supporting wall; an animal cell has no wall and may swell and burst in sufficiently dilute surroundings. In concentrated surroundings cells lose water and shrink; plant tissue may become less firm. These effects follow water movement, not movement of sugar into the cell.

CELL BIOLOGY · MILESTONE 10 OF 12

Required Practical 2: Osmosis
Why am I learning this?

Comparing potato mass in different solutions tests an osmosis prediction. Fair measurements and graphs help distinguish a real effect from experimental error.

What should I already understand?

Osmosis theory and its predictions about water movement.

Previous: Osmosis
Next recommended: Active transport

Analysing mass changes and graphs

Percentage change in mass = (final mass − initial mass) / initial mass ×100. For 2.0 g becoming 2.3 g, change is +0.3 g and percentage change is +15%; for 2.5 g becoming 2.0 g, it is −20%. A negative sign records loss; a percentage is not a mass in grams. Mean rate of water uptake can be estimated from mass gain / time when other mass changes are negligible: 0.30 g in 20 min = 0.015 g/min = 15 mg/min. This is an average, not proof that uptake was constant. Blotting consistently reduces surface-water error. Plot solution concentration on the horizontal axis and percentage mass change on the vertical axis, with labels, units, a suitable even scale and both gains and losses. For example, results at 0, 2, 4 and 6 g sugar per 100 mL of final solution of +15%, +5%, −5% and −15% cross zero between 2 and 4, approximately 3 g/100 mL. Use an appropriate trend line and interpolate; do not force it through the origin. Near the zero-change concentration, the solution and tissue have no net water exchange under the conditions (approximately isotonic). Water still moves both ways. This estimates the tissue's equivalent solute concentration; it does not show cells have stopped all transport, identify each solute, or give an exact value beyond the data precision. Use more concentrations near the crossing to improve the estimate. Practise plotting the separate dataset below before viewing its graph.

Preparing for the physical required practical

Investigate the effect of a range of salt or sugar concentrations on plant-tissue mass (AQA Trilogy required practical 2).

Review the theory in the previous milestone. Follow your teacher’s safety instructions in the laboratory. Reading this guidance or using the Osmosis Lab does not complete the physical required practical.

Experimental method

RP02 investigates how a range of salt or sugar solution concentrations affects the mass of plant tissue. Use the same type/source of plant tissue, for example potato cylinders cut with the same borer and trimmed to equal length; equal dimensions help control surface area and diffusion distance. A teacher prepares/carries out cutting or supervises use of a borer/scalpel on a safe surface; cut away from fingers, use eye protection as instructed and follow school sharps procedures. Do not taste laboratory materials; clean spills to prevent slips and wash hands. Label a range of known solution concentrations and use the same solution volume for each. Record concentration units consistently, such as g sugar per 100 mL final solution. Gently blot each sample in the same way, measure initial mass on a suitably precise balance and record dimensions if needed to check consistency. Immerse samples fully for the same time at the same temperature, using separate repeat samples at each concentration. Remove them, blot consistently without squeezing out internal water, and record final mass. Keep tissue source, dimensions, immersion time, temperature and solution volume controlled. Initial/final length can provide supplementary observations but does not replace the required mass measurements. Calculate final minus initial mass, then percentage change using initial mass as the denominator. This permits fairer comparison when initial masses differ slightly. Calculate each repeat's percentage change before taking a mean; record spread and investigate unexpected values. Plot mean percentage change against concentration, include negative results, and use an appropriate line/curve of best fit to estimate where it crosses zero. A point is not discarded merely for being inconvenient: investigate a recorded cause, repeat it, and explain any exclusion. More independent repeats improve reliability; closer concentration intervals near zero improve the concentration estimate. A finer balance may reduce measurement uncertainty; repeating an unchanged biased procedure does not remove its systematic error.

Controls and fair comparisons

Same tissue source and dimensions; equal solution volume, temperature and immersion time; consistent blotting and balance procedure. Independent repeat samples at each concentration; record and investigate anomalies.

Analysing results and evaluating errors

Worked example: initial 2.0 g, final 2.3 g gives +0.3 g and +15%. Initial 2.5 g, final 2.0 g gives −0.5 g and −20%. If +0.30 g is gained in 20 minutes, mean water-uptake estimate = 0.015 g/min. Example graph: +15, +5, −5, −15% at 0, 2, 4, 6 g/100 mL crosses zero near 3 g/100 mL. This is an estimate under those conditions, not proof that water molecules stop moving.

Use initial mass, not final mass, as the percentage denominator. Surface solution can inflate final mass. Plot concentration horizontally and percentage vertically; do not force the trend through the origin or extrapolate beyond the data without justification. Recording length alone does not complete this mass investigation.

What should I demonstrate?

Plan controlled measurements and repeats; calculate percentage mass change, interpret graphs and evaluate errors.

CELL BIOLOGY · MILESTONE 11 OF 12

Active transport
Why am I learning this?

Roots absorb minerals even from dilute soil, and the gut absorbs glucose against a gradient. These jobs require cells to use energy.

What should I already understand?

Diffusion, osmosis and the respiration-energy introduction below.

Previous: Required Practical 2: Osmosis
Next recommended: Cell Biology assessment

Before active transport: energy from respiration

Respiration releases energy from glucose in cells. Energy transferred by respiration powers cell processes; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration. Moving a substance against its concentration gradient requires this energy supply. Compare that with diffusion and osmosis, which do not require energy from respiration.

Transport against a gradient

Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient and requires energy transferred by respiration. Root hair cells can absorb mineral ions from dilute soil water this way.

Active transport and comparisons

Active transport uses energy supplied by respiration to move dissolved substances from a lower concentration to a higher concentration, against the gradient. Root-hair cells can accumulate mineral ions from dilute soil water, helping healthy growth even when their internal ion concentration is greater. Small-intestine cells can absorb glucose from a lower concentration in the gut into blood with a higher glucose concentration; glucose supplies respiration. Diffusion alone cannot sustain uptake against that gradient. Compare the processes: diffusion can move dissolved substances or gases down their own gradients without energy from respiration; osmosis moves water across a partially permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution without energy from respiration; active transport moves substances against their gradient and requires respiration energy. Decide from the substance, membrane, direction and energy evidence rather than assuming every root-uptake process is active transport: water enters by osmosis.

What should I demonstrate?

Compare active transport with diffusion and osmosis; explain mineral and glucose uptake and their energy requirement.

Cell Biology assessment

Explaining ideas without reading a model answer reveals what you understand and what needs another look. This brings cell structures, growth and transport together.

What should I already understand?

All eleven earlier milestones; revisit any freely before answering.
